opus-5.5.text:
I think they're really quite different, and the difference is more fundamental than people usually appreciate. Reinforcement learning is about understanding your world. It's about an agent that has goals, takes actions, sees what happens, and learns from that experience to do better. That's what I'd call basic AI: figuring out what to do in order to achieve your goals.

Large language models are about mimicking people. They learn to predict what a person would say in a given situation. That's a very different thing. They're not learning from their own experience of acting in the world and seeing the consequences. They're learning from a huge corpus of text that people produced, and they're trying to imitate it.

People will say the LLMs have a world model, but I'd question that. They have a model of what people would say. A real world model would let you predict what will actually happen when you do something, and then you'd be surprised when it doesn't, and you'd learn from that surprise. LLMs don't really have that. There's no ground truth in the normal course of their operation, no notion of a right action defined by a goal, so there's nothing for them to be corrected against.

That's really the key point for me: without a goal, there's no sense of better or worse. In reinforcement learning, there's a reward, and that gives meaning to what's right and wrong. Next-token prediction isn't a goal about the world. It doesn't change the world, and the model doesn't care what happens next in any substantive sense.

And I'd connect this to the bitter lesson. In some ways LLMs look like a triumph of scaling general methods with lots of computation, but they're also leaning heavily on human knowledge, all that human-generated text. My expectation is that, as has happened over and over in AI history, the methods that learn from experience, that can scale with computation without being bottlenecked by what humans have already written down, will eventually supersede the ones that depend on human knowledge.

r001.rationale: It characterizes reinforcement learning as an agent learning to understand its world through action and experience.

r002.rationale: It says large language models learn to mimic people by predicting what a person would say.

r003.rationale: It contrasts LLMs with goal-directed action, saying they lack a goal or notion of a right action and do not learn what to do to achieve goals.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think they're really quite different in their fundamental orientation. Reinforcement learning is about understanding your world. It's about an agent that has goals, that takes actions, that sees the consequences of those actions, and learns from them. The agent is trying to figure out how the world works so it can get what it wants. That's the core of it. There's a goal, there's experience, and there's learning from that experience.

Large language models are about mimicking people. They're trained to predict what a person would say next. And that's a very different thing. They don't have a goal in the sense that I mean. Predicting the next token isn't a goal about the world; it's a goal about matching a dataset. They're not learning from the consequences of their actions in the world. They're learning from a static record of what humans have written.

Now, people will say, well, the language model must have built a world model in order to predict text so well. And I'd push back on that. A world model, in my sense, is something that lets you predict what will happen if you do something. The language model predicts what a person would say, not what the world will do. Those get conflated a lot, but they're not the same. To have a world model you need to be able to be surprised by the world, and then to update. The language model has no ground truth to be surprised by once it's deployed. It can't be wrong about anything, because nothing happens.

And this connects to what I wrote in The Bitter Lesson. The lesson there was that methods that scale with computation win out over methods that build in human knowledge. People read the language model success as a confirmation of that, and in one sense it is, because they use a lot of computation. But in another sense, a large language model is the ultimate case of building in human knowledge. The whole thing is human knowledge. All of it comes from us. So I think it's actually a bit of a detour, a very impressive detour, but a detour, from the path of building agents that learn from their own experience.

The real test is: can the system keep learning on its own, continually, from what happens to it? That's what animals do. That's what children do. A squirrel doesn't learn by imitating a large corpus of squirrel behavior. It learns by trying things and seeing what works. I think that's the thing we still haven't cracked, and I think the language model approach, for all its successes, isn't aimed at cracking it.

r001.rationale: It says reinforcement learning is about an agent trying to understand how the world works.

r002.rationale: It describes large language models as mimicking people by predicting what a person would say next.

r003.rationale: It contrasts an agent choosing actions to achieve goals with language models that predict human speech and says they lack that kind of goal.

astra-6.text:
The distinction I would emphasize is learning from examples versus learning from the consequences of your actions. In reinforcement learning, an agent interacts with the world, takes actions, and learns to obtain more reward. It has to discover what to do, including when an action’s benefits don’t show up until much later.

The basic training of a large language model is different. You give it text and train it to predict the next token. That’s a powerful way to learn about the structure of language and, indirectly, about the world. But the training objective is to predict what appears in the data. It isn’t, by itself, to discover through interaction how to achieve a goal.

These aren’t mutually exclusive approaches. You can use reinforcement learning to train a language model. A language model can also be a component of an agent that acts and learns. So the important question is where the learning ultimately comes from: are we learning to reproduce human-generated examples, or are we learning from our own experience what works?

I think the latter is essential. We want systems that can keep learning, that can encounter something people haven’t already explained to them and figure out how to deal with it.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning learns from interactions and consequences to obtain rewards, but does not characterize its aim as understanding the world.

r002.rationale: It describes language models as learning to reproduce human-generated examples, which communicates mimicking people.

r003.rationale: It says next-token prediction is not, by itself, about discovering through interaction how to achieve a goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is learning to act versus learning to imitate. A language model is trained, primarily, to predict the next token in text produced by people. Reinforcement learning asks: How should an agent act so that the consequences of its actions are better, as measured by some reward signal?

Those can overlap. You can use reinforcement learning to train a language model, and you can use prediction as part of a reinforcement learning agent. So these aren’t mutually exclusive technologies. But they suggest different ways of approaching intelligence.

In reinforcement learning, the agent interacts with the world. It takes an action, something happens, and it learns from that experience. Crucially, it has to deal with consequences that may come much later. An action might look good immediately and turn out to have been a mistake.

With language models, we’ve gotten a tremendous amount out of learning from what people have already written. But I’m interested in systems that can continue learning from their own experience, that can discover things we don’t already know. I think that ability to learn toward a goal through interaction is central to intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning as learning to act toward better reward through interaction, but does not characterize its aim as understanding the world.

r002.rationale: It says language models learn to predict text produced by people and contrasts that with learning to act, clearly describing imitation of people.

r003.rationale: By describing language models as trained primarily to predict people’s text and contrasting this with reinforcement learning’s focus on how to act, it communicates that LLMs are not aimed at figuring out what to do.
